newsitem.title: FRANCE: LVMH loses 1st round in bitter Sauternes war.
newsitem.headline: LVMH loses 1st round in bitter Sauternes war.

text.p: Count Alexandre de Lur Saluces has won the first round of a court battle to block the huge luxury goods conglomerate LVMH from taking over the famed Chateau d'Yquem vineyard held by his family since 1785.

A court in the southern city of Bordeaux blocked the sale of the property to LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton on Thursday and rejected its request for a mediator but agreed to freeze the assets until the dispute is resolved.

"This ruling was not a judgment on the core issue in the dispute, which is whether Eugene de Lur Saluces had the right to sell his share," said a spokeswoman for LVMH. "That case could last a long time."

LVMH announced in November it had struck an agreement with Eugene de Lur Saluces, Alexandre's brother, and other members of the family to acquire 55 percent of Chateau d'Yquem, which produces one of France's finest wines, a sweet, golden Sauternes traditionally served with foie gras (fatted goose liver).
Alexandre de Lur Saluces, who has managed the property for 28 years, was travelling at the time and heard about the sale of the ancestral property on the radio.
He has challenged the 500 million franc ($90 million) deal on the grounds that it required both brothers' approval. Eugene de Lur Saluces says he is not bound by a joint-ownership agreement.
He asked the Bordeaux court to order an independent appraisal of his brother's management of the property but was turned down in Thursday's ruling.
The court agreed, however, to LVMH's request to freeze the assets to prevent Alexandre de Lur Saluces from striking an alternative deal, the LVMH spokeswoman said.

The David-versus-Goliath struggle is being followed like a soap opera in France. LVMH chairman Bernard Arnault is viewed as a brilliant businessman, but tough in his dealings with the small, mostly family-owned luxury firms which he has acquired to turn LVMH into the industry leader worldwide.

LVMH, whose portfolio includes some of France's finest brands -- Christian Dior, Moet Chandon and Guerlain to name a few -- recently carried out a contentious takeover in the United States of the upscale retail chain Duty Free Shoppers.

Minority owner Robert Miller last week accused LVMH of reneging on a deal to buy his 38.75 percent share in DFS and said he expected to take court action. He had previously failed in efforts to stop LVMH from acquiring control of DFS.
Arnault said last week, during a presentation of LVMH's 1996 results, that he would not buy out Miller for the time being.

He said he had made repeated overtures to Alexandre de Lur Saluces, promising to retain the traditional wine-making process and inviting him to stay on to manage the property, but said Lur Saluces had refused to even see him.

"Yquem should not be relegated to the ranks of banal products," Lur Saluces told the newspaper Liberation. He said LVMH's profit-oriented strategy was incompatible with Chateau d'Yquem's goal of making an exceptional wine.

Sauternes wines, of which Yquem is generally acknowledged to be the best, are made from grapes that are left on the vine until they start to rot, concentrating the sugar. The grapes are then picked off by hand. In bad years, no wine is produced.
Rare old Yquems sell for thousands of dollars a bottle. ($ = 5.668 French Francs)
